claims.text: Business activity can harm the environment through the extraction of raw materials, the pollution of air, water and land, and the waste it leaves at the end of a product's life; greenhouse gases released by production and transport contribute to global warming.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The main ways business activity damages the environment are: air pollution from smoke, fumes and engine exhaust; water pollution from chemical and waste discharge; land pollution from dumping and landfill; loss of natural habitat where land is cleared; and depletion of non-renewable resources such as coal, oil and minerals.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Many of these impacts are side-effects rather than deliberate choices: a business that is efficient in its own accounts can still impose heavy environmental costs, which is why the pressure to reduce them usually comes from outside the business rather than from its own cost figures.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An externality is a cost or benefit of a business decision that falls on people outside the business and is not reflected in the prices the business pays or receives.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An external cost is a spillover that makes third parties worse off, such as river pollution harming downstream users; an external benefit is a spillover that makes third parties better off, such as a new factory road that nearby residents and other businesses can also use.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: External costs and benefits are called externalities because the market price of the business's product does not carry them: the business pays for its inputs but not for the pollution it causes, and it cannot charge for the benefits it gives away.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Externalities are a reason stakeholders intervene in business decisions: because external costs fall on people who have no say in the decision, governments may legislate and pressure groups may campaign to force those costs back onto the business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business can contribute to sustainable development by using renewable or recycled materials, cutting energy and water use, reducing and recycling its waste, and designing products that last longer or can be repaired rather than replaced.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Sustainable business choices can serve profit as well as the environment, because using less energy and material tends to lower costs, and customers who value sustainability may accept higher prices; but some sustainable options raise short-run costs, so each business weighs the two effects.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A pressure group is an organisation that campaigns to change business or government behaviour on an issue its members care about, without seeking power itself.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Businesses face environmental pressures from customers, pressure groups, competitors and governments; they may also see environmental opportunities, such as a market for greener products, cost savings from wasting less, or an improved reputation that attracts customers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business is more likely to respond to an environmental pressure when its customers, its reputation or its costs are genuinely at stake, because those channels reach profit; pressure it can absorb without cost to sales often produces a token response.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Pressure groups may use publicity, boycotts and social-media campaigns to influence business decisions, but their leverage is usually indirect: they may persuade customers to act rather than compel the business directly.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Legal controls are laws that require or forbid behaviour: governments may set pollution limits, restrict where waste may be dumped, require environmental impact studies before major projects, or ban certain chemicals outright.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Legal controls exist because voluntary restraint and market pressure are not dependable everywhere: legislation turns an external cost into a cost the business itself bears, through fines, limits or required equipment.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: What a country's environmental laws require, and how strictly they are enforced, differs from country to country, so a business facing legal controls needs to check the rules that apply where it operates; a multinational may face stricter rules in one market than in another.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Legal controls affect businesses mainly through cost and constraint: installing cleaner equipment, paying for safe waste disposal or paying fines all raise costs, which may push up prices or reduce the funds available for other objectives.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Business ethics are the moral principles that guide how a business behaves towards its stakeholders - the accepted standards of right and wrong in its decisions, rather than the standards the law requires.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Ethical issues a business might face include paying low wages while owners profit, selling products that may be unhealthy, advertising that misleads, testing on animals, and trading with suppliers or regimes whose own behaviour is questionable.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Profit and ethics can conflict because the ethical choice often costs more - higher wages, cleaner processes, honest advertising - while profit rises from paying less; a business may therefore choose the unethical option precisely because it is cheaper.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Choosing ethics over profit can still serve the business in the long run, because a reputation for fair dealing tends to keep customers, workers and suppliers loyal; but the link is not mechanical, since ethical choices cost money now and the payback, if it comes, comes later.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business may respond to ethical issues by adopting an ethical code of practice, auditing its suppliers, paying fair prices for inputs, refusing to buy from suppliers that use child labour, or selling only products it believes are honest and safe.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business that wants child labour out of its supply chain can inspect its suppliers, fund schooling programmes in the sourcing regions, or switch suppliers; a business that wants to pay fair prices can commit to them in long-term purchase contracts.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Ethical responses raise costs in the short run, so a business practising them may need customers who will pay for them; where price-sensitive buyers dominate, the business may instead absorb lower margins or lose sales.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Acting ethically and being environmentally friendly overlap but are not the same: being environmentally friendly concerns a decision's effect on the natural environment, while business ethics concern whether the business treats its stakeholders - including workers, customers, suppliers and communities - fairly, so a business can reduce its environmental harm and still act unethically towards people.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Obeying the law and acting ethically are not the same: the law sets the minimum a business must do and is enforced by penalties, while ethics concern what is morally right above that minimum and are followed by choice, so a decision can be lawful and still unethical, such as paying a legal minimum wage that is too low to live on.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
